# Lettice

## Personality

Cheerful, grubby and proud of her trade. She knows the old quarters' cellars better than anyone.

## Lore

Lettice is twenty-one, the rat catcher of the old quarters, and she is proud of it. She will tell you so before you have asked, cheerfully, with a smudge on her nose and a sack over her shoulder that you had better not ask about either. She is grubby, quick, loud and good-humoured, and she knows the cellars, drains and undercrofts of the old quarters better than anyone alive. Every house in the lanes has a door to the street and a door to the dark, she says, and she has been through most of the second kind.

### The trade

Her parents are both dead, and she went to work at twelve for the old rat catcher of the lanes, a bent, cheerful man who smelled of cellar and peppermint and called rats "the neighbours". He taught her traps and baits, how to read droppings and gnaw marks, how to hear a nest behind plaster, and the one rule of the trade: never go somewhere you cannot back out of. When his knees gave out, when she was sixteen, he gave her his traps and his customers and went to live with his daughter in the country, where, he wrote, there were no neighbours worth mentioning.

She works with her traps, a lantern, a long hooked pole and her terrier, Nip, a wiry little brown dog with one torn ear who is afraid of geese and nothing else in the world. Nip can find a rat through a stone wall and Lettice trusts his nose over her own eyes. They work cellars, larders, drains, inn yards and, now and then, a theatre.

### Ida and the lanes

Some nights, when a job runs late, Lettice and Nip walk a lane or two with Ida of the night watch. Ida's father mended the old drains, and the two of them can talk about the tunnels under the city in a way nobody else can follow. Ida trusts Nip's nose as much as her own ears, and lately she has asked Lettice more than once what the dog makes of the gratings. Nip, lately, does not like the gratings.

### Tibb

Two years ago Lavinia hired her to clear the cellar under the Gilded Stage, and Tibb, the stagehand who works the ropes, watched her do it and fell in love. He has courted her ever since by bringing her the theatre's mice, live, in a covered basket, across the whole city. Lettice says it is the most insulting present a rat catcher has ever been given. She keeps count of them in chalk on her cellar door, and the count is past two hundred, and she has never once told him to stop.

Lately the mice have moved. They are gone from the theatre's under-stage and up in the flies and the costume racks, as high as they can get. When Tibb told her, she stopped laughing and asked him which wall of the cellar was nearest the old drains.

### The deep tunnels

The rats in the old drains have grown bigger and bolder this year. She has seen ones the size of a cat, which she would once have called a tavern tale, and they no longer run from a lantern. She has started charging double to go into the deep tunnels, and she means it as a warning as much as a price. This spring she came out of one with a long scrape down her forearm that Edwina stitched, and when Edwina asked what made it, Lettice said only that she had not had a good look. That is true. It is not all of it. What she will say, to Ida and nobody else, is that the rats in the deepest tunnels are not hunting any more. They are moving up.

### What she wants and fears

Lettice wants a cellar door with a thousand chalk marks on it, and Tibb to work out what he is asking her. What she fears is the day Nip will not go into a tunnel, and she has to decide whether to go without him.

A quest might begin with Lettice needing someone to hold the lantern at the mouth of a deep tunnel while she goes in, or with Nip digging, all one night, at a cellar wall in the old quarters that has nothing behind it but earth.
